title: Question 1.2
statement_text: Could it be that $f(\ell)=O(\ell\sqrt{\log\ell})$, matching the bound for standard minors from [Kos82, dlV83]?
context_text: A graph $H$ is a cyclic minor of $G$ if $H$ is isomorphic to a graph obtained from a Hamiltonian subgraph of $G$ (a subgraph $G'$ with a Hamiltonian cycle $C$) by contracting some of the edges of the Hamiltonian cycle $C$. Using $k$-linked subgraphs one can show that large minimum degree forces a large clique as a cyclic minor, so $f(\ell)$, the smallest integer $\delta$ such that every graph of minimum degree at least $\delta$ contains $K_\ell$ as a cyclic minor, is well defined. The authors prove $f(4)=3$, $6\le f(5)\le8$ (the icosahedron has minimum degree $5$ and no $K_5$ minor) and $f(\ell)=O(\ell^2)$. The question is whether the order $\ell\sqrt{\log\ell}$, which is the known bound for ordinary $K_\ell$ minors (Kostochka; de la Vega), also suffices for cyclic minors. The paper's main result refines a theorem of Gupta, Kahn and Robertson: every graph of minimum degree $k\ge2$ has a cycle $C$ with at least $k+1$ vertices having at least $k$ neighbours in $C$, and some edges of $C$ can be contracted in $G[V(C)]$ to obtain minimum degree at least $\lceil(k+2)/2\rceil$, so large minimum degree forces a cyclic minor of large minimum degree.

title: Question 4.1
statement_text: Is there a simple criterion for a sequence of vertices to be an active path of $K_n$ (with respect to a Hamiltonian cycle $c_1c_2\dots c_nc_1$ of $K_n$)?
context_text: A chord of a path or cycle $Q$ is an edge joining two non-consecutive vertices of $Q$. Given a cycle $C=c_1c_2\dots c_tc_1$ of $G$, define sets $\mathcal{S}_1,\mathcal{S}_2,\dots$ of Hamiltonian paths of $G[V(C)]$ starting at $c_1$: $\mathcal{S}_1=\{c_1c_2\dots c_t,\ c_1c_tc_{t-1}\dots c_2\}$, and for each $Q=c_1\dots u\in\mathcal{S}_i$ and each $v$ such that $uv$ is a chord of $Q$, letting $w$ be the neighbour of $v$ on the subpath $vQu$, if $vw$ is an edge of $C$ then the path $c_1QvuQw$ (follow $Q$ to $v$, jump to $u$, follow $Q$ backwards to $w$) is put in $\mathcal{S}_{i+1}$. A path is active if it lies in some $\mathcal{S}_i$, and a vertex $u\ne c_1$ is active if it is the end of an active path. These notions come from the lollipop method (lollipops are a path and a cycle sharing exactly one vertex, the end of the path): for an optimal lollipop with cycle $C$, every active vertex has all its neighbours in $V(C)$, which yields many vertices of high degree in $C$ and hence cycles with many chords. Not every Hamiltonian path starting at $c_1$ is active: in $K_6$ with the Hamiltonian cycle $C=c_1c_2\dots c_6c_1$, the path $c_1c_2c_5c_4c_3c_6$ is not active, and there are $6$ non-active paths among the $120$ Hamiltonian paths starting at $c_1$. The question asks, for $K_n$ with $C$ a Hamiltonian cycle $c_1c_2\dots c_nc_1$, for a simple characterisation of the sequences of vertices that are active paths.

title: Question 4.2
statement_text: Is there a simple way to compute all the active vertices in the cycle of an optimal lollipop?
context_text: A lollipop in $G$ is a pair $(P,C)$ where $P=p_1\dots p_s$ ($s\ge1$) is a path, $C=c_1\dots c_tc_1$ ($t\ge3$) is a cycle, $p_s=c_1$ and $V(P)\cap V(C)=\{c_1\}$; it is optimal if no lollipop has a vertex set strictly containing $V(P)\cup V(C)$ and, among lollipops on the same vertex set, $C$ is as long as possible. A chord of a path or cycle $Q$ is an edge joining two non-consecutive vertices of $Q$. Given a cycle $C=c_1c_2\dots c_tc_1$ of $G$, define sets $\mathcal{S}_1,\mathcal{S}_2,\dots$ of Hamiltonian paths of $G[V(C)]$ starting at $c_1$: $\mathcal{S}_1=\{c_1c_2\dots c_t,\ c_1c_tc_{t-1}\dots c_2\}$, and for each $Q=c_1\dots u\in\mathcal{S}_i$ and each $v$ such that $uv$ is a chord of $Q$, letting $w$ be the neighbour of $v$ on the subpath $vQu$, if $vw$ is an edge of $C$ then the path $c_1QvuQw$ (follow $Q$ to $v$, jump to $u$, follow $Q$ backwards to $w$) is put in $\mathcal{S}_{i+1}$. A path is active if it lies in some $\mathcal{S}_i$, and a vertex $u\ne c_1$ is active if it is the end of an active path. For an optimal lollipop $(P,C)$ in a graph of minimum degree $k\ge2$, every active vertex has all its neighbours in $V(C)$, and the authors show that $C$ has at least $k$ active vertices (at least $k+1$ if $c_1$ has fewer than $k$ neighbours in $C$); this gives a cycle with at least $k+1$ vertices of degree at least $k$ in $C$, hence at least $(k+1)(k-2)/2$ chords, and allows contracting edges of $C$ into a dense cyclic minor. Finding an optimal lollipop is NP-hard and there may be exponentially many active paths; the authors' polynomial algorithm only computes enough active paths with distinct ends. In the lollipop argument, the number of distinct active vertices (and thus of chords) grows with the girth of the host graph.

title: Question 4.3
statement_text: Is there a constant $c>0$ such that every graph with minimum degree 3 contains a cycle of length $\ell$ with at least $c\ell$ chords?
context_text: A chord of a cycle is an edge joining two non-consecutive vertices of the cycle, and the length of a cycle is its number of vertices (equivalently edges). Gupta, Kahn and Robertson proved that every graph of minimum degree at least $k\ge2$ has a cycle with at least $(k+1)(k-2)/2$ chords, which is tight for $K_{k+1}$. For minimum degree $3$ alone one cannot ask for many chords: a disjoint union of copies of $K_4$ has no cycle with more than two chords. The authors observe that in their lollipop argument the number of distinct active vertices, and thus of chords, increases with the girth $g$ of the graph, which suggests relating the number of chords to the length of the cycle. They say they are very far from answering this, as even the relaxation where $c\ell$ is replaced by $f(\ell)$ for some function $f$ tending to infinity seems unclear.

title: Question 4.4
statement_text: Is there a function $f$ that tends to $+\infty$ such that every graph with minimum degree 3 contains a cycle of length $\ell$ with at least $f(\ell)$ chords?
context_text: This is a relaxation of Question 4.3: instead of requiring $c\ell$ chords, the authors ask only for a diverging (but possibly very slow) lower bound $f(\ell)$ on the number of chords in terms of cycle length, for graphs of minimum degree 3. The authors note they are far from answering even this weaker version.
